slide_text: Inventing Big O Notation Some programs finish in a blink. Others take hours — or years. In this chapter you'll discover why by measuring, counting, and eventually inventing a notation that captures it all. Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

Challenge (skip ahead if you can): Write a function that estimates the Big O class of any function . It should count steps (not time) at each input size, then report which growth class fits best. [code block] [code block] Already got it? The next slides will guide you step by step.
Part 1: How Long Does It Take? You've written functions. Some are fast, some are slow. But how slow? And what happens when the input gets bigger? Let's find out by measuring.

Here are two functions. adds up all the numbers in a list (one loop). checks whether any two numbers in the list add up to a target (a loop inside a loop). [code block] We'll pass a target of -1 to . Since all our numbers are positive, no pair will ever add up to -1 — this forces the function to check every pair before giving up, so we measure its full workload.

Time It Time both functions on lists of size 1,000 , 5,000 , and 10,000 . For each size, record how long each function takes. When the input gets 5× bigger (1,000 → 5,000), how much slower does each function get? Use before and after each call to measure: [code block] Try the same for n = 5000 and n = 10000. Hint 1 Create a list with for the larger size. Wrap each function call with before and after, then subtract to get the elapsed time. Hint 2 When the input grows 5x (from 1,000 to 5,000), should take roughly 5x longer. But should take roughly 25x longer. Why 25? Because 5 squared is 25.
Plot the Growth Plot time vs input size for both functions on the same graph. Use input sizes from 100 to 5,000. What shape does each curve have?

One function's time grows proportionally to the input size. The other grows proportionally to the square of the input size. This distinction is enormous. On a million items: The linear function takes ~1 second The quadratic function takes ~ 11 days Understanding which category your algorithm falls into is one of the most important skills in programming.

Part 2: Counting Steps Timing is noisy — it depends on your computer's speed, what else is running, even the room temperature. Can we predict how an algorithm grows without running it? Yes: count the key operations .

Does the Constant Matter? Write two functions that both loop through a list once, but one does 3× as much work per element. For example, one adds each element once, the other adds it three times. Time both on sizes 10,000, 100,000, and 1,000,000. Compute the ratio of their times for each size. Does the ratio stay constant or change as n grows?

We care about the growth rate , not the exact count. Whether it's [math], [math], or [math] — they all grow at the same rate. Whether it's [math], [math], or [math] — they all grow quadratically. We need a shorthand that captures the growth family and throws away the constants. How would you write "this algorithm grows like n²"?

Quick Check — Counting Steps A function has a single loop that runs n times, and inside the loop it does 5 operations per iteration. How does the total number of operations grow as n gets larger? A. It grows like 5 (constant) B. It grows like n (linear) C. It grows like 5n (five times linear) D. It grows like n² (quadratic) Answer: B. The total operations are 5n, but since 5 is just a constant multiplier, the growth rate is the same as n. Doubling n doubles the work, regardless of the constant.
Part 3: Inventing a Notation You keep saying things like "this grows like n" or "this grows like n squared." Let's make that precise.

Invent a Shorthand You keep writing "this algorithm grows like n²" or "grows like n·log(n)." That's wordy. Invent a shorter way to write it. The notation you just invented is called Big O notation . Computer scientists write: $[math][math]O(f(n))[math]f(n)[math]O(n^2)[math]n^2$. The formal notation was introduced by Paul Bachmann in 1894 and popularised by Edmund Landau — but the idea is exactly what you discovered: classify algorithms by their growth family, ignore the constants.

Quick Check — Reading Code Complexity What is the Big O of this function? [code block] A. O(n) — because the first loop is O(n) B. O(n + n²) — because there is an O(n) loop and an O(n²) nested loop C. O(n²) — because the nested loop dominates D. O(n³) — because there are three loops total Answer: C. The first loop is O(n) and the nested pair is O(n²). Total is n + n² but we keep only the fastest-growing term, so the answer is O(n²).

Part 5: Memory Complexity Time isn't the only resource that matters. Memory (space) does too. The same Big O notation works — instead of asking "how does time grow?" we ask "how much extra memory does this algorithm need as the input grows?"

How Much Extra Space? For each function, figure out how much extra memory it creates (beyond the input itself). Don't count the input list — just the new things the function allocates. Function A: [code block] Function B: [code block] Function C: [code block] For each: how many new items does it create? How does that depend on n? Function A — new items created: Function B — new items created: Function C — new items created: Hint 1 For Function A, count the variables it creates beyond the input. is just one number, no matter how big the list is. Hint 2 Function B builds a new list with one element per input element: n new items. Function C creates n rows, each with n items, so n times n = n² new items.

See the Space Grow Create lists of increasing size and n×n matrices of increasing size. Count the number of elements in each to verify the growth pattern. For lists: how does the element count grow with n? For matrices: how does the element count grow with n?

The Time–Space Tradeoff You need to check if a list has any duplicate values. Here are two approaches: Approach 1 — Nested loops (no extra memory): [code block] Approach 2 — Use a set (extra memory): [code block] What's the time complexity of each? (Think about the loop structure.) What's the space complexity of each? (How much extra memory does each create?) Which is "better"? Approach 1 — time / space: Approach 2 — time / space: Which is better and why: Hint 1 Approach 1 has a loop inside a loop (nested). Approach 2 has a single loop plus a set. Checking for a set takes O(1) on average. Hint 2 Approach 1: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Approach 2: O(n) time, O(n) space. It uses more memory to get much faster. That is the tradeoff.

Every algorithm has both a time complexity and a space complexity. Now you know how to read and evaluate both. As you work through the chapters ahead, you'll see this tradeoff again and again — fast algorithms that use extra memory vs slow algorithms that work in-place.

Quick Check — Space Complexity A function takes a list of n numbers and creates a new dictionary where each number maps to its square. What is the space complexity? A. O(1) — dictionaries are always constant space B. O(n) — the dictionary has one entry per input element C. O(n²) — dictionaries use more space than lists D. O(log n) — dictionaries use hashing, which is logarithmic Answer: B. The dictionary stores n key-value pairs, one for each input element. The extra memory grows in direct proportion to n.

fragments.text: Nobody taught you Big O — you derived it yourself . The next time someone says "this algorithm is O(n log n)," you know exactly what it means and why it matters.

slide_text: Going further: O(2 ) — exponential: The number of subsets of a set with n items. Algorithms that try every subset are O(2 ) — feasible for n up to about 20, impossible for n = 100. O(n!) — factorial: The number of permutations. Even worse than exponential. Amortized analysis: Some operations are usually fast but occasionally slow (like appending to a Python list that needs to resize). Amortized analysis averages the cost over many operations. P vs NP: The biggest open question in computer science — are there problems where checking a solution is easy but finding one is fundamentally hard? A million-dollar prize awaits the answer.
Part 8: Reflection — What Did You Just Build?

Reflection Answer these questions in your own words: Why do we count operations instead of measuring wall-clock time? What problems does timing have that counting avoids? Explain in your own words what O(n²) means. Why does an O(n²) algorithm become impractical much sooner than an O(n) algorithm? A friend says "my algorithm does 3n + 100 operations, so it is O(3n + 100)." What would you tell them, and why? Give a real-world example (outside of programming) where something grows linearly vs quadratically. For instance, what grows linearly and what grows quadratically when you invite more people to a party? You saw that using a set to check for duplicates trades O(n) memory for O(n) time (instead of O(n²) time). When might you choose the slower O(n²) approach on purpose? If you had to explain Big O notation to a friend who has never programmed, what analogy or everyday example would you use?
